title: Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah House
summary: The Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah house was used by Pharoah later in his life. The house featured two "Indian barns" as food storage, and a footpath toward Bridgehampton on it's edge. The foundation remains today, but the house may have been a wood cabin during its use.
map_geometry_source: Broad public orientation point on Old Tar Road from prior WP reference and reverse geocoding; not the house foundation or route.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: The surviving foundation of Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah’s home, which famously included traditional subterranean "Indian barns" for food storage, offers a rare glimpse into nineteenth-century Native domestic life. Highlighting these everyday architectural adaptations demonstrates how Indigenous individuals actively sustained longstanding survival practices even as modern development rapidly encroached on their homelands.
history_content: Historic interpretation at the Talkhouse ruins describes the foundation stones as the remains of what is thought to have been the house of Stephen "Talkhouse" Pharoah, one of the best-known Montaukett figures in East Hampton history. Nearby shallow pits, often called "Indian barns" in local tradition, were likely covered with woven thatch and used for food storage. Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah was born in Springs in 1819, at Molly's Hill, and was a direct descendant of Montaukett Chief Wyandanch. Local accounts describe his childhood indenture, his work on a whaling ship, his time in California during the Gold Rush, his Civil War service with the 29th Connecticut Volunteers, and his later reputation as the fastest walker on the East End. Residents paid him to carry mail, and P.T. Barnum promoted him as "The World's Greatest Walker." In 1878, Pharoah began a lawsuit seeking property rights to Indian Fields in Montauk for Montaukett people. He died of tuberculosis in 1879 and was buried at Indian Fields Cemetery in Montauk. Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah should be remembered as a Montaukett person whose public reputation, labor, walking feats, and family history made Native presence visible during an era of land loss and displacement. Because the source record concerns a house site and family landscape, exact coordinates are not shared.
preservation_content: Learning With Care: Exact coordinates for house ruins, family places, or burial-related locations are not shared. The public history is kept at a broad Montaukett and East Hampton landscape scale.
